kid.question: When did the Lord say He first knew Jeremiah?

options.text: Before Jeremiah was born
When Jeremiah began school
When Jeremiah became king
After Jeremiah left home

kid.explanation: The Lord says He knew Jeremiah before forming him in the womb and appointed him a prophet to the nations.

kid.question: Why did Jeremiah think he could not speak for God?

options.text: He thought he was too young
He thought he lived too far away
He thought he had lost his voice
He thought he must first become king

kid.explanation: Jeremiah calls himself a child when he protests that he cannot speak.

kid.question: What was Jeremiah told to say to the people?

options.text: Whatever the rulers requested of him
Whatever the Lord commanded him
Whatever his neighbors suggested to him
Whatever the priests voted to teach

kid.explanation: The Lord tells Jeremiah to go where He sends him and speak what He commands.

kid.question: What promise helped Jeremiah face people without fear?

options.text: The people would all welcome him
The king would speak for him
His family would travel with him
The Lord would be with him

kid.explanation: The Lord promises His presence and deliverance, rather than promising a friendly audience.

kid.question: What did the Lord touch when calling Jeremiah?

options.text: Jeremiah's shoulder
Jeremiah's forehead
Jeremiah's mouth
Jeremiah's hands

kid.explanation: The Lord touches Jeremiah's mouth and says He has put His words there.

kid.question: Which pair of jobs is part of Jeremiah's calling?

options.text: Buying and selling
Building and planting
Fishing and sailing
Singing and dancing

kid.explanation: Along with pulling down and destroying, Jeremiah is commissioned to build and plant.

kid.question: From which direction would trouble come upon the land?

options.text: From the south
From the east
From the north
From the west

kid.explanation: After the vision of the boiling pot, the Lord says evil will break forth from the north.

kid.question: What had the people worshipped instead of the Lord?

options.text: The stars shining above them
The rivers flowing through valleys
The rulers living among them
Things made by their hands

kid.explanation: The judgment concerns forsaking God, burning incense to other gods, and worshipping their own handiwork.

kid.question: Which object pictures how strong Jeremiah would be made?

options.text: A stone tower
A bronze shield
An iron pillar
An oak beam

kid.explanation: The Lord describes Jeremiah as a defended city, an iron pillar, and bronze walls.

kid.question: What past help had the people stopped asking about?

options.text: God leading them out of Egypt
God helping them build a ship
God sending them a new king
God giving them a city wall

kid.explanation: The people failed to ask about the Lord who brought them out of Egypt and led them through the wilderness.

high-school.question: How is the period of Jeremiah's prophetic ministry framed?

options.text: By Egypt's plagues and Israel's wilderness journey
By temple festivals and successive priestly appointments
By Judah's kings and Jerusalem's captivity
By Assyria's victories and Nineveh's eventual repentance

high-school.explanation: The opening dates the word of the Lord by Josiah, Jehoiakim, and Zedekiah, ending with Jerusalem's captivity.

high-school.question: How does the Lord answer Jeremiah's concern about his age?

options.text: His commission waits for further years of public training
His commission passes to an older member of his family
His commission begins after the people approve his message
His commission rests on God's prior knowledge and command

high-school.explanation: God's knowledge and appointment precede Jeremiah's birth; his youth does not cancel the command to go and speak.

high-school.question: How do the promised presence and the touching of the mouth equip Jeremiah?

options.text: God supplies both royal approval and a public audience
God supplies both protection and the message to speak
God supplies both priestly rank and a temple residence
God supplies both military command and plans for defense

high-school.explanation: God promises to be with him to deliver him and places His words in Jeremiah's mouth.

high-school.question: What is the scope of the work described by the six action verbs?

options.text: It concerns repairing and enlarging the walls around Jerusalem
It includes dismantling and establishing among nations and kingdoms
It includes harvesting and storing the produce of Judah's farms
It concerns appointing and training the priests within the temple

high-school.explanation: The commission combines destructive verbs with building and planting, and its stated scope is nations and kingdoms.

high-school.question: What does the Lord's response to the almond-rod vision emphasize?

options.text: He will delay until Jeremiah's fears have passed
He will replace speaking with a written record
He will act to carry out His word
He will reserve His word for the next generation

high-school.explanation: The Lord interprets the vision by saying He will hasten His word to perform it.

high-school.question: How do the pot vision and the judgment speech fit together?

options.text: A southern drought brings judgment for Judah's neglected farming
An eastern migration fulfills Judah's request for new neighbors
A western invasion fulfills Judah's plan to expand its borders
A northern threat brings judgment for Judah's forsaking God

high-school.explanation: The threat comes from the north, and the Lord identifies forsaking Him and worshipping other gods as grounds for judgment.

high-school.question: What does the Lord promise when commanding Jeremiah to speak boldly?

options.text: Opponents will hear him and immediately become his supporters
Opponents will fight him but will not overcome him
Opponents will appoint him to govern in the king's place
Opponents will leave him to address the priests in private

high-school.explanation: The Lord names opposition from across the land, yet says it will not prevail because He is with Jeremiah.

high-school.question: What memory introduces the Lord's complaint against Israel?

options.text: Early prosperity while trading with the surrounding kingdoms
Early skill while building the sanctuary in Jerusalem
Early devotion while following Him through the wilderness
Early courage while choosing a king from among them

high-school.explanation: God remembers the kindness of Israel's youth and bridal love in following Him in an unsown wilderness.

high-school.question: What contrast exposes Israel's response to God's generosity?

options.text: He brought them to fertile land that they then defiled
He kept them in desert land that they then cultivated
He gave them foreign cities that they then refused
He led them to coastal towns that they then abandoned

high-school.explanation: The Lord recalls wilderness deliverance and a plentiful country, then charges the people with defiling His land.

high-school.question: Why does the comparison with other nations intensify the charge?

options.text: Israel exchanged its glory although nations retain their gods
Israel kept its customs although nations constantly change theirs
Israel sought new prophets although nations had none to consult
Israel rejected foreign trade although nations welcomed its merchants

high-school.explanation: The question about nations changing gods highlights the astonishing exchange of Israel's glory for what cannot profit.

expert.question: What does the opening chronology establish about the received word?

options.text: Its restriction to one king's brief season of religious renewal
Its arrival after the captives had already returned to Jerusalem
Its continuity across reigns into the catastrophe of captivity
Its dependence on changes in the hereditary priestly office

expert.explanation: The word comes across several named reigns, with the chronological endpoint being Jerusalem's captivity.

expert.question: What relationship joins prenatal appointment to the command to speak?

options.text: Prior divine purpose authorizes service despite perceived inadequacy
Prior divine purpose supplies a reason to postpone public service
Perceived inadequacy requires the transfer of prophetic authority
Perceived inadequacy limits the message to Jeremiah's own household

expert.explanation: God's prior knowledge and appointment counter Jeremiah's self-description as a child and lead directly to commanded action.

expert.question: How does the symbolic act at Jeremiah's mouth relate to his authority over kingdoms?

options.text: The entrusted word underlies both judgment and constructive commission
The entrusted word authorizes Jeremiah to command the defending armies
The symbolic touch restricts judgment to those holding priestly office
The symbolic touch appoints Jeremiah to select the next king

expert.explanation: God puts His words in Jeremiah's mouth immediately before commissioning him to uproot, destroy, build, and plant.

expert.question: What differs in the explanations attached to the two visions?

options.text: One authorizes the message; the other promises safety from the threat
One assures fulfillment; the other identifies the direction of threat
One identifies the threatened city; the other names its conqueror
One postpones divine action; the other commissions Jeremiah to rebuild

expert.explanation: The almond-rod vision concerns God's performing His word; the boiling-pot vision introduces evil from the north.

expert.question: How is the announced military threat given a moral interpretation?

options.text: Foreign rulers' arrival is joined to judgment on abandoned allegiance
Foreign rulers' arrival is joined to praise for Judah's renewed worship
The besieged gates are treated as evidence of failed construction
The besieged gates are treated as grounds for replacing the priests

expert.explanation: Northern kingdoms place thrones at Jerusalem's gates, and God explains His judgments in terms of forsaking Him and worshipping handmade gods.

expert.question: How should the fortified-city imagery be read beside the final promise?

options.text: It describes a future building project for the royal household
It equips a contested messenger rather than removing opposition
It assigns the prophet a defensive post under Judah's commanders
It announces immediate agreement among all the groups addressed

expert.explanation: City, pillar, and walls portray Jeremiah's God-given firmness; the next verse explicitly says opponents will fight him.

expert.question: What does the opening relational and agricultural imagery recall?

options.text: Israel's military beginnings and authority over neighboring nations
Jerusalem's architectural beginnings and suitability for royal residence
Israel's devoted beginnings and consecrated status before the Lord
Jerusalem's commercial beginnings and dependence on foreign harvests

expert.explanation: Bridal love in the wilderness and firstfruits belonging to God recall devotion and consecration, not political or commercial beginnings.

expert.question: How does the wilderness recollection sharpen the accusation of defilement?

options.text: Deliverance follows the people's successful cultivation of the wilderness
The land's infertility excuses the people's pursuit of other providers
The land's abundance proves the people's continued covenant obedience
Deliverance and provision precede the people's corruption of the gift

expert.explanation: God led Israel through a dangerous wilderness into a plentiful country, which they then defiled. The recollection makes their response a betrayal of generosity.

expert.question: What unites the failures attributed to the different leadership groups?

options.text: Religious responsibilities are transferred from priests to foreign rulers
Religious responsibilities coexist with failure to know and follow God
Legal expertise compensates for the prophets' lack of public authority
Legal expertise makes the pastors' disobedience a private matter

expert.explanation: Priests fail to seek the Lord, law handlers do not know Him, pastors transgress, and prophets speak by Baal.

expert.question: What is the force of comparing Israel's exchange with other nations' practice?

options.text: Frequent changes of foreign gods explain Israel's political vulnerability
Foreign refusal to worship shows why Israel must reduce its ceremonies
Foreign prosperity demonstrates that Israel has chosen a better exchange
Loyalty to powerless gods exposes disloyalty to Israel's true glory

expert.explanation: Other nations do not change their gods, although those are no gods; Israel has exchanged its glory for what does not profit.
